Trustworthy Evaluation of AI-Assisted Painting Restoration

Metric and Region-Policy Ablation Study

controlled_50 23 ablation scenarios Painting is the independent unit Three complete core models Bounded SDXL diagnostics No universal trust score

1. Executive findings

This study tested whether the thesis conclusions survive reasonable changes to metrics, evaluation regions, operational thresholds, and flag aggregation. Model ordering was stable. Case priorities and screening flags were much more sensitive.

Ranking scenarios 18 / 18 LaMa remained a winner
Most stable omission 10 candidates changed without CLIP
Outside-mask case agreement 0.097 Spearman correlation with baseline
More-sensitive thresholds +1,285 triggered flag rows
  • LaMa remained first under every complete, omitted-family, single-family, and region-policy ranking. The overall computational model conclusion is therefore robust.
  • Classical metrics alone tied LaMa and Telea. Classical similarity is therefore not sufficient to separate those methods under this population.
  • Outside-mask-only and boundary-only policies substantially reordered cases. They are useful diagnostics, but poor replacements for the complete region policy.
  • Lower flag counts often accompanied more insufficient evidence. Fewer flags must not be interpreted as better restoration without checking evidence coverage.
Conclusion. The main model conclusion is robust, but individual-case screening depends materially on which evidence and regions are available. Trustworthy evaluation therefore needs the complete transparent framework.
Limit. These conclusions apply to the controlled_50 evidence and the declared computational metrics. They do not establish historical authenticity or conservation approval.

2. What was tested

The analysis evaluated 23 predeclared scenarios: twelve metric configurations including the baseline, six region policies, two threshold policies, and three aggregation rules. Restoration and feature inference were not rerun.

Population Cases Candidates Use
Core matched ranking population 410 1230 Three-model quality and case-rank sensitivity
Nonzero quality population 360 1080 Family-balanced ordinal ranking
Complete flag union 410 1785 Candidate-level flag stability
Bounded SDXL subset 10 10 Separate flag diagnostics only

RQ1 — Evidence beyond traditional similarity

Metric-family ablations test whether classical, perceptual, feature, texture, colour, seam, spatial, semantic, and uncertainty evidence contribute distinct conclusions.

RQ2 — Conditional model comparison

Model and case ranks are recomputed under reasonable alternatives to determine which comparisons remain stable.

RQ3 scope extension — Uncertainty-aware screening

Uncertainty is removed only from supported stochastic flags. It is never assigned artificially to deterministic methods or used in the cross-model quality rank.

Conclusion. The experiment tests evaluation-policy sensitivity rather than restoration-model inference sensitivity.
Limit. The 1,785-candidate flag union contains primary, repeated-seed, uncertainty-only, and bounded SDXL roles. Those roles remain separate and are not treated as independent models.

3. The complete evaluation framework

The baseline uses eleven quality anchors from ten evidence families and 36 operational indicators. Each evidence family contributes equally to model ranking after painting-level aggregation.

Model Baseline rank Evidence families Quality anchors
LaMa 1.0 10 11
OpenCV Telea 2.0 10 11
Stable Diffusion 3.0 10 11
  • LaMa ranked first.
  • OpenCV Telea ranked second.
  • Stable Diffusion ranked third.
  • All 50 zero-damage controls remained explicitly unranked.
  • Runtime and uncertainty were excluded from cross-model quality ranking.
Conclusion. The baseline preserves complementary evidence instead of compressing it into a universal score. LaMa is the strongest core model under this declared computational framework.
Limit. Family-balanced rank is a descriptive comparison. It does not convert metric evidence into a conservation decision.

4. Metric-family ablation

Removing one metric family rarely changed the three-model order, but it often changed case priorities or flag states. Single-family configurations produced the largest evidence losses.

Scenario Changed candidates Triggered-flag change Case-rank rho Winner
Complete approved framework 0.0% +0 1.000 LaMa
Without classical metrics 14.9% +203 0.998 LaMa
Without LPIPS 34.0% +44 0.998 LaMa
Without CLIP 0.6% -10 1.000 LaMa
Without DINOv2-derived evidence 99.3% -261 0.991 LaMa
Without texture evidence 85.7% -70 0.997 LaMa
Without colour evidence 21.0% +69 0.997 LaMa
Without seam evidence 85.7% -119 0.994 LaMa
Without uncertainty evidence 37.0% -37 1.000 LaMa
Classical metrics only 100.0% -1,916 0.974 LaMa / Telea
Perceptual metrics only 100.0% -1,896 0.928 LaMa
Semantic and feature evidence only 100.0% -1,436 0.912 LaMa
  • Removing CLIP changed only 10 candidates and left case ordering almost unchanged (rho 0.9996). CLIP had the least independent influence in this ablation.
  • Removing DINOv2-derived evidence changed 1,773 candidates. DINOv2-related semantic and structural evidence therefore carries substantial screening information.
  • Classical-only evidence changed every candidate and tied LaMa with Telea. Traditional metrics alone weakened model separation and removed important diagnostic coverage.
  • Perceptual-only and semantic/feature-only configurations retained LaMa but changed every candidate's flag state. A stable winner does not mean the evaluation remained equivalent.
Conclusion. Complementary metric families matter more for case review and failure screening than for the broad three-model order.
Limit. A family omission changes evidence availability as well as the resulting flags. Reduced trigger counts cannot be read as improved restoration performance.

5. Region-policy ablation

Region policies changed which aspects of a restoration were measured. No single restricted region reproduced the complete framework for both ranking and screening.

Scenario Changed candidates Triggered-flag change Case-rank rho Winner
Full image only 99.8% -168 0.910 LaMa
Content region only 95.3% +400 0.924 LaMa
Masked pixels where valid 99.5% -1,661 0.872 LaMa
Mask bounding-box crop only 94.5% +311 0.953 LaMa
Boundary regions 99.8% +1,032 0.381 LaMa
Outside-mask regions 100.0% -1,671 0.097 LaMa
  • The mask-bounding-box policy had the highest case-rank agreement among restricted regions (rho 0.953). It was the closest restricted substitute, but still changed 94% of candidate flag profiles.
  • Boundary-only evidence reduced case-rank agreement to 0.381. Boundary diagnostics therefore emphasize a different set of difficult cases.
  • Outside-mask-only evidence reduced agreement to 0.097 and moved the median case rank by 109.25 places. It cannot replace restoration-region evidence.
Conclusion. The complete region policy is necessary because mask, crop, boundary, full-image, and outside-mask regions answer different restoration questions.
Limit. Region metrics are comparable only within their declared semantics. A boundary result and a masked-region result do not measure interchangeable properties.

6. Threshold sensitivity

Operational quantiles were shifted in both directions while leaving the evidence values unchanged.

Scenario Changed candidates Triggered-flag change Case-rank rho Winner
More sensitive thresholds 51.7% +1,285 Not applicable Not applicable
More specific thresholds 35.3% -900 Not applicable Not applicable
  • More-sensitive thresholds added 1,285 triggered flag rows and changed 923 candidates. They identify more cases for review but increase screening burden.
  • More-specific thresholds removed 900 triggered rows and changed 630 candidates. They reduce alerts but risk missing moderate adverse evidence.
Conclusion. Threshold choice changes review volume substantially. The approved thresholds should be treated as operational screening settings, not objective failure boundaries.
Limit. These quantiles are not calibrated probabilities and were not validated against expert labels.

7. Aggregation-rule sensitivity

Aggregation ablations changed how independent indicator warnings became transparent candidate-level flags.

Scenario Changed candidates Triggered-flag change Case-rank rho Winner
One warning or one critical 44.8% +1,079 Not applicable Not applicable
Three warnings or one critical 20.1% -371 Not applicable Not applicable
Critical indicators only 22.1% -420 Not applicable Not applicable
  • One warning or one critical indicator added 1,079 triggered rows and changed 799 candidates. This rule is more cautious but less selective.
  • Three warnings or one critical indicator removed 371 triggered rows and changed 358 candidates.
  • Critical-only aggregation removed 420 triggered rows and changed 395 candidates. It suppresses warning-level evidence rather than proving those candidates are safe.
Conclusion. Aggregation rules control screening strictness. The complete rule retains warning accumulation while allowing one critical indicator to trigger review.
Limit. Flag aggregation is transparent decision support, not a learned or expert-validated diagnostic classifier.

without_texture texture_inconsistency 85.7% -349 1785

Metric-disagreement, semantic, structural, texture, seam, and outside-mask flags were especially sensitive when their source evidence or required region was removed.

The large blue regions in the heatmap do not automatically represent improvement. Many coincide with explicit insufficient-evidence states.

Conclusion. Flag stability is evidence-dependent by design. A trustworthy report must show why a flag changed, not only whether its trigger count rose or fell.
Limit. The flags are computational rules. They are not human ratings, historical truth, or conservation ground truth.

9. Model and case-rank stability

LaMa remained a winner in all 18 ranking scenarios. Only the classical-only scenario produced a tie with Telea. Stable Diffusion remained third in every tested ranking configuration.

Case ranking behaved differently. Metric omissions generally retained high agreement, while boundary-only and outside-mask policies reordered the diagnostic queue substantially.

Conclusion. The thesis can make a robust broad model comparison within the controlled population, but case-level review priority must retain the complete evidence policy.
Limit. Ordinal case ranks identify relative diagnostic difficulty. They are not continuous quality scores or case trust scores.

10. Subgroup stability

Descriptive summaries were retained only when at least five independent paintings contributed to the subgroup.

Subgroup dimension Scenario–subgroup rows Levels Minimum paintings Maximum paintings
damage_fraction 276 12 5 50
damage_or_degradation_type 115 5 5 50
experiment 92 4 5 50
painting_category 115 5 10 10
prompt_arm 69 3 50 50
seed_coverage_role 92 4 5 50
  • All six declared subgroup dimensions passed the minimum painting-count gate for at least one level.
  • Category summaries contain limited paintings and remain category–painting confounded.
  • Prompt-arm and seed-coverage summaries preserve their population roles rather than treating repeated candidates as independent paintings.
Conclusion. Policy sensitivity is not uniform across every subgroup, but the available category evidence is descriptive rather than a general style-effect test.
Limit. Five-painting groups support controlled description only. They do not establish broad category or style generalization.

12. Thesis synthesis, limits, and provenance

RQ1

Complementary evidence families materially affect failure screening and case ordering. Traditional similarity alone is insufficient.

RQ2

LaMa remains the strongest core model under every tested ranking policy, but case-level priorities depend on the full metric and region framework.

RQ3 scope extension

Removing supported uncertainty evidence changes stochastic screening but correctly leaves deterministic cross-model quality ranking unchanged.

Supported conclusions

  • LaMa has the most stable overall computational ranking in the controlled population.
  • Metric families and evaluation regions provide non-interchangeable evidence.
  • Case prioritization and operational flags are policy sensitive and must remain transparent.
  • Missing evidence cannot be interpreted as successful restoration.
  • The framework supports human review; it does not replace conservation judgement.

Claims not supported

  • historical authenticity;
  • physical conservation suitability;
  • museum approval;
  • human-rated visual quality;
  • calibrated probabilistic confidence;
  • full-dataset SDXL superiority or inferiority;
  • a universal trust score.

Limit. All results inherit the controlled dataset, synthetic-damage, pretrained-feature, partial SDXL, and computational-ground-truth limitations declared by the upstream notebooks.
